news.content: New avian influenza tools for poultry industry on horizon Work has started on numerous research projects to help the poultry industry better protect itself from HPAI. Mark Clements July 29, 2026 Kharkhan_Oleg | iStock.com Poultry producers can expect to benefit from numerous new tools over the next few years to help protect their businesses from losses associated with highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI). To help give the industry the options it needs, various research projects are underway in the U.S. with support of the U.S. Department of Agriculture Animal and Plant Inspection Service. Following a competitive process, the agency awarded more than $100 million to a wide range of research projects late last year. The funded projects are designed to advance prevention, therapeutics, vaccine development and research about transmission and potential biosecurity solutions for HPAI. Looking into light At Columbia University, work into far-ultraviolet C light received funding. Among objectives of the study is to determine how susceptible the HPAI virus is to far-ultraviolet C exposure. David Welch, assistant professor of radiation oncology at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons and leader of the study, explained: "We already know that far-ultraviolet C is very effective in inactivating viruses such as coronavirus and other influenza viruses, and we expect similar efficacy for avian influenza." The important parameter for efficacy is the dose of ultraviolet light, which is the product of the intensity of the far-ultraviolet C light and the exposure time, he continued. Exposing the virus to an intense source would allow for quicker inactivation. The university is working with a far-ultraviolet C fixture made by biosecurity technology company Visium, designed for use in agricultural settings. Lamps will be installed in a barn filled with chickens at Texas A&M University, with performance monitored over time. The far-ultraviolet C lighting will be fixed to the ceiling throughout the house providing coverage similar to visible lighting. Another project goal is to evaluate the impacts of dust on far-ultraviolet C exposure. The ceiling-mounted lamps will point downward to minimize dust accumulation and protected from water and dust intrusion, which offers the cleaning option of simply spraying them should it be necessary. The far-ultraviolet C light emitted is not within the range visible to birds, meaning the lamps can be left on 24 hours a day to provide continuous protection. Current versions of far-ultraviolet C lamps use excimer bulbs which have an estimated lifetime of at least 11,000 hours — approximately 15 months of continuous operation. Only having the lights on when the barn is in use would extend the time between changing bulbs, Welch noted. Promising advances in light-emitting diode technology will, hopefully, enable far-ultraviolet C light-emitting diodes to become a viable option for these applications, he continued. Insects: Vectors and vaccines Other funded research projects focus on how the virus may be entering the house and could offer producers new tools to protect their houses from the outside. Very local routes of infection are under examination through work being carried out at St. Jude's Children's Research Hospital, where the team of researchers has experience in influenza virology, veterinary medicine and wildlife veterinary medicine. Project leader Richard Webby, member of the Department of Host Microbe, is working with Carol Cordona, professor, Department of Veterinary and Biomedical Sciences at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, and Justin Brown, associate teaching professor program coordinator, Undergraduate Studies, Veterinary & Biomedical Sciences of Pennsylvania State College of Agricultural Sciences. Among areas being studied is whether and how insects might bring the virus into poultry houses. Traps have already been laid on farms to find out which insects are present. The team will look at how an insect carrying the virus might transmit the infection, for example, by walking over the wet surface of an eye of a bird. The study will also look at the role of songbirds in virus spread. While much work has already been carried out in this field, this is not the case for the currently circulating virus strain. Chukars and pheasants will also be studied to determine why the HPAI virus tends to affect these birds to different degrees. Another avenue of study by the group is the role of fomites, for example dust and water, in HPAI and how the virus behaves when in contact with them. This should result in a better understanding of how the virus might travel from a pond into the poultry house. With work already underway, some results should be available within the next few months and, it is hoped, by project end, it should be possible to inform producers of where they should implement greater insect control and whether greater insect control programs need to be carried out during the bird migration season. While the work at St. Jude's is looking at keeping insects and other vectors out, work at Kansas State University is looking at introducing them in the form of modified mealworms that act as a vaccine delivery method. The modified mealworms could be given as a feed supplement, quickly protecting thousands of birds without the need to handle them. By using gene editing, Kansas State University researchers can quickly update mealworm vaccines to match circulating strains as the virus mutates. Airborne approach Investigation of the aerosolized antiparasitic niclosamide to control and treat HPAI is being carried out at Purdue University. The project is looking at using niclosamide as both a prophylactic and a therapeutic and builds on work carried out at the university in niclosamide use for human health. Niclosamide, currently authorized by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration as an oral anthelmintic medication to primarily treat tapeworm infection, has anti-cancer and antiviral properties. What has held its development back has been its poor solubility. However, thanks to new technology developed by Purdue University professor Yuan Yao's group, its solubility has been increased by more than 5,000 times. Yao, the leading principal investigator in this new work against HPAI, notes that work on niclosamide's use against HPAI began earlier this year and that the university is in the process of building a fogging facility to realize niclosamide's entry into birds' respiratory tracts via water droplets. Niclosamide alters the biological conditions of host cells rather than directly attacking the virus, making infection more difficult. Once chickens are fogged, niclosamide distribution within the respiratory tract will be analyzed to understand how much fogging is needed to achieve sufficient drug distribution for protection. Once parameters are established, HPAI challenge trials will be carried out at a collaborating university. If the research is successful, fogging birds with niclosamide could be used in two different ways, Yao explained. It could be administered therapeutically when disease symptoms appear in a flock or preventatively if a HPAI outbreak occurs on a neighboring farm. analysis.time: Published on July 29, 2026. Research projects are underway with results expected within the next few months.
analysis.location_and_population: Poultry producers and their flocks are the primary population affected.
analysis.event: Multiple research projects are underway to develop new tools for preventing and managing highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in the poultry industry. These projects are funded by the U.S. Department of Agriculture Animal and Plant Inspection Service.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Over $100 million has been awarded for research projects. The projects aim to advance prevention, therapeutics, vaccine development, and biosecurity solutions for HPAI. No specific case counts or death tolls are mentioned.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Research is ongoing at institutions including Columbia University, St. Jude's Children's Research Hospital, Kansas State University, and Purdue University. Some results are expected within the next few months. The source is a full original report body.

analysis.brief_en: The U.S. poultry industry is set to benefit from new tools to combat highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), with over $100 million in research funding awarded by the USDA. Projects focus on diverse approaches: Columbia University is testing far-ultraviolet C light for virus inactivation in barns; St. Jude's is investigating insect vectors and fomites; Kansas State is developing modified mealworms as a vaccine delivery method; and Purdue is exploring an aerosolized antiparasitic, niclosamide. These initiatives aim to provide producers with innovative prevention and treatment options, with preliminary results anticipated in the coming months.

analysis.brief_en: Victoria, Australia has reported its first case of the highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu strain, marking a significant public health development. The detection, confirmed by local authorities, underscores the potential threat of avian influenza to both animal and human populations. While details about the affected individual, source of exposure, and potential transmission routes remain limited, this case highlights the importance of ongoing surveillance and biosecurity measures. Health officials are expected to release further information regarding response actions and risk assessment. The emergence of H5N1 in Victoria serves as a reminder of the global challenge posed by avian influenza viruses and the need for vigilant monitoring to prevent widespread outbreaks.

Britannica Editors Last updated July 30, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Early detection of bird flu is important in preventing and controlling outbreaks. One way the virus can be detected is by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), in which nucleic acids from blood or tissue samples are analyzed for the presence of molecules specific to bird flu. Other methods include viral antigen detection, which detects the reaction of antibodies to viral antigens in samples of skin cells or mucus, and viral culture, which is used to confirm the identity of specific subtypes of influenza based on the results of PCR or antigen detection and requires growth of the virus in cells in a laboratory. Tests based on lab-on-a-chip technology that take less than an hour to complete and can accurately identify specific subtypes of bird flu are being developed. This technology consists of a small device (the “chip”) that contains on its surface a series of scaled-down laboratory analyses requiring only a tiny volume of sample (e.g., picolitres of saliva). These chip-based tests, which are portable and cost-effective, can be used to detect different subtypes of influenza in both poultry and humans. Vaccine development Because of the many immunologically distinct viral subtypes that cause influenza in animals and the ability of the virus to rapidly evolve new strains, preparation of effective vaccines is complicated. The most effective control of outbreaks in poultry remains rapid culling of infected farm populations and decontamination of farms and equipment. This measure also serves to reduce the chances for human exposure to the virus. In 2007 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a vaccine to protect humans against one subtype of the H5N1 virus. It was the first vaccine approved for use against bird flu in humans. It was not intended for commercial use; rather, it was stockpiled to provide some measure of protection against a future outbreak of bird flu. The vaccine also was only moderately effective, necessitating ongoing development of improved agents. Out of those efforts emerged a second vaccine, which used an adjuvant substance to boost the immune response. The vaccine was approved in 2013 by the FDA, and similar to the first vaccine, it was not made commercially available and instead was added to the national stockpile. Scientists continued to work to develop a vaccine that is effective against another subtype of H5N1, as well as a vaccine that might protect against all subtypes of H5N1. In 2023–24, growing concerns about the potential for sustained human-to-human transmission, along with advances in vaccine technology, fueled interest in the development of an mRNA vaccine against H5N1. The introduction of technology based on messenger RNA (mRNA) offered opportunities for the accelerated generation of more effective vaccines. Studies suggest that antiviral drugs developed for human flu viruses would work against bird flu infection in humans. The H5N1 virus, however, appears to be resistant to at least two of the drugs, amantadine and rimantadine. Britannica Editors History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything This article was originally published May 15, 2020, and updated October 15, 2020.When a global outbreak of disease begins to slow, feelings of relief and a sense of moving on ensue. But historically, based on past pandemics involving diseases like the plague, cholera, and influenza, that feeling of security has been short-lived. Pandemic diseases, once clear of their initial peak of activity and seemingly on their way out, have a tendency to re-emerge in a different segment of the population and spread anew, giving rise to a second wave of disease.In the modern era, public health experts have warned that highly contagious infectious diseases, including pandemic influenza and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), have the potential to re-emerge and produce second and possibly even third waves of disease. And these subsequent rounds of disease are sometimes worse than the first. The influenza pandemic of 1918–19 occurred in three waves, which took place over the course of a year. Whereas the first wave of that pandemic did not deviate noticeably from typical influenza epidemiology, the second and third waves were unusually deadly for 20- to 40-year-olds. The influenza (H1N1) pandemic of 2009 had two waves, the second of which caused significantly more illness than the first.There was much speculation about whether a second wave of disease would sweep the world during the COVID-19 pandemic. To investigate this possibility, scientists developed models of different intervention scenarios and found that the likelihood of an additional round of illness and death by COVID-19 increased significantly when interventions to limit the spread of disease were relaxed. In particular, experts warned, the premature reopening of the economy in areas where new cases of disease continued to be reported all but ensured that a second wave would happen.China, where the COVID-19 outbreak was first detected, was the first country to move past the initial wave of disease, a milestone of relief that came in the first half of February 2020. But, just weeks after newly reported cases dropped to zero in many places in China, researchers became concerned about re-emergence of the disease particularly in areas where restrictions on social distancing and travel had been eased. These concerns were realized in mid-May, when a cluster of new COVID-19 cases was detected in western Wuhan, after a stretch of just 35 days without new infections. Related Topics: pandemic COVID-19 (Show more) See all related content In late September 2020, while countries such as the United States and India were still in their first wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, health officials declared the emergence of a second wave of the disease in Europe. In most European countries, daily cases were higher during the second wave, compared with the first. news.content_title: Australia Confirms `Some Local Spread' of H5N1 - CSIRO Testing An Additional 11 Samples From SA
news.content: " I can advise that today the consultative committee on animal diseases, emergency animal diseases met and has agreed based on testing and sequencing by the CSRO lab that some local transmission has occurred between a number of greater crested terns that are resident in South Australia. While there remains no evidence of any mass mortalities at this point in time, we do expect with this local transmission that there will be further detections in Australian wildlife. " - From Transcript of remarks by Agriculture Minister Julie Collins #19,267 Overnight South Australia updated their avian flu web portal , announcing that another 11 presumed positive samples have been sent to CSIRO for confirmation and genetic testing. Current situation South Australia’s first confirmed detection of H5 bird flu was in a wild migratory bird (southern giant petrel) on Wednesday, 24 June at Knights Beach at Port Elliot on the Fleurieu Peninsula. Further confirmed detections include a giant petrel (8 July at Hardwicke Bay, Yorke Peninsula); a southern giant petrel (10 July at Emu Bay, Kangaroo Island); a northern giant petrel (10 July at Port Vincent, Yorke Peninsula); three greater crested terns (10 July at Robe, Limestone Coast; 26 July at Semaphore, metro Adelaide; and 26 July at Robe, Limestone Coast); and seven greater crested terns (28 July at Cape Jaffa, Port MacDonnell and Southend, Lower South East). A further 11 suspected H5 bird flu detections are undergoing further confirmatory testing at the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness in Victoria. The strain of virus is consistent with the strain detected in the Southern Indian Ocean Sub-Antarctic Territories, including Heard Island. This strain has not been detected in poultry and has not become established in any part of Australia. Up-to-date national information is available at birdflu.gov.au . This comes just 1 day after CSIRO confirmed 7 new cases in local seabirds from the state's southeast Limestone Coast. The results of those tests also strongly suggest local transmission of the virus has occurred among native birds. Although disappointing, none of this is particularly surprising. The history with HPAI H5 - particularly since the emergence and subsequent evolution of the 2.3.4.4x clade - has been that it travels well in migratory birds, and that when it reaches new territories, it often finds suitable native hosts. While the situation in Australia continues to evolve, so far there are no reports of spillovers into poultry. On Monday I shared an X/Twitter post by Professor Raina Macintyre showing the recent H5N1 detections overlaid on a map of Australia's poultry production regions. Yesterday, the above mentioned data was published in a preprint on bioRxiv . HPAI H5N1 risk in Australia: a model for the prediction of poultry outbreaks Pan Zhang, Samsung Lim, Ashley Quigley, C Raina MacIntyre doi: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.07.27.740638 This article is a preprint and has not been certified by peer review Preview PDF Abstract The panzootic highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 virus has now been detected on the Australian mainland, with incursions from the sub-Antarctic region posing an increasing threat to domestic wildlife and poultry populations. Our study aimed to predict the risk of HPAI H5N1 poultry outbreaks across Australia at the local government area (LGA) level using a range of influential risk factors. We first used a Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) model to estimate the environmental suitability for HPAI H5N1 occurrence across Australia. The resulting suitability layer was then integrated with five additional predictor layers, including abundance data for two Southern Ocean wild birds, one of which has introduced HPAI H5N1 into Australia; abundance data for 28 native Australian wild birds; native bird flyways across Australia; Australian chicken density; and poultry farm density. The six layers were aggregated and averaged to generate an HPAI H5N1 risk map for poultry outbreaks across Australian LGAs. Although most incursions have occurred in Western Australia (WA) and South Australia (SA), we identified New South Wales (NSW) and Victoria (VIC) as having the highest predicted risk of HPAI H5N1 poultry outbreaks . Additional high-risk areas were identified in WA, SA, and Tasmania (TAS) . In contrast, the Northern Territory (NT) and large parts of Queensland (QLD), WA, and SA were predicted to be at low risk. These findings provide a spatially explicit framework to support targeted surveillance, preparedness, and biosecurity measures aimed at mitigating the impact of future HPAI H5N1 outbreaks in Australian poultry. The Australian government has provided a number of resources for both commercial and backyard poultry producers to help improve their biosecurity

news.content: From alert to action: How New Zealand is responding to H5N1’s arrival Opinion by Jemma Geoghegan & Nigel French NZ Herald· 4 mins to read Jemma Geoghegan is Professor and Webster Family Chair in Viral Pathogenesis, University of Otago; Nigel French is Distinguished Professor of Infectious Disease Epidemiology and Public Health, Te Kunenga ki Pūrehuroa – Massey University Subscribe to listen Access to Herald Premium articles require a Premium subscription. Subscribe now to listen. For now, detection rates are low, but ongoing surveillance of H5N1 will be essential to determine whether additional cases emerge. Photo / Getty Images The first cases of the highly pathogenic avian influenza virus H5N1 in New Zealand mark an important milestone, but not an unexpected one. Since the virus reached Australia last month, and as it continued its global spread, scientists and government agencies have been preparing for the possibility that itwould eventually arrive here. For now, detection rates are low, but ongoing surveillance of H5N1 will be essential to determine whether additional cases emerge. Australia provides an important indication of what New Zealand may face. H5N1 was detected in a brown skua in Western Australia less than four weeks ago. Further detections followed in Western Australia and South Australia, mainly in migratory seabirds, with a detection subsequently reported in New South Wales. More recently, H5N1 was confirmed in a greater crested tern in South Australia, marking the first detection in a resident Australian seabird, and therefore a possible indication of local transmission. So far, the Australian detections have involved individual seabirds rather than widespread wildlife mortality. The virus has not been detected in poultry in Australia. Susceptibility to infection and severe disease varies between species and individual incursions in solitary scavenging or predatory seabirds may not lead to widespread infection. The risk of transmission is likely greatest in populations that live in large colonies, particularly at high density. These can be a source of transmission to other species that inhabit the same environments — for example, shorebirds and marine mammals such as seals and sea lions. Proximity to backyard poultry and other livestock populations then becomes critical for onward transmission to domestic animals. How prepared is New Zealand? The advantage for New Zealand is that we are not facing this blindly. The experiences of Australia and the rest of the world have provided several years of information about how H5N1 behaves, which species may be most susceptible and which surveillance and response approaches are most effective. New Zealand has also spent recent years strengthening surveillance programmes, diagnostic capacity and collaboration between wildlife, agricultural and public health agencies. These systems will now be tested in practice. No country can be completely prepared for a virus with such a broad host range and capacity to move over long distances in wild birds. However, early detection, rapid information sharing and clear co-ordination between agencies will give New Zealand the best opportunity to understand and reduce the impacts of the virus. Priorities for the response The immediate focus should be on determining the scale and distribution of infection. This means increasing surveillance around the initial detection, testing potentially affected wildlife, and rapidly sharing information between laboratories, wildlife managers, veterinarians, public health authorities and affected communities. Enhanced biosecurity measures and clear public communication will also be essential, building on preparedness plans developed by the Ministry for Primary Industries, the Department of Conservation, Health New Zealand and regional authorities. The Department of Conservation has trialled a vaccine developed for poultry on five of our critically endangered taonga species of wild bird (takahē, kākāpō, black stilts, shore plovers and red-crowned kākāriki). The vaccine is safe and results in an immune response that is likely to be protective. As a consequence, the Ministry for Primary Industries has approved the vaccine for use in these species, and this is now being rolled out on a larger scale. However, it requires two doses and can only be practically implemented in captive, managed populations or on offshore islands. The devastating impact of the virus on marine animals, such as the northern and southern elephant seals, reminds us of the vulnerability of New Zealand populations of seals and sea lions, including the pakake/New Zealand sea lion. In the US, trials of a bird flu vaccine formulated for cattle have been carried out in the endangered Hawaiian monk seal. While the trials show promise, we are a long way from using these in marine mammals in Aotearoa. Genomic sequencing will be particularly important. It can help identify where the virus likely originated, whether New Zealand has experienced one or several introductions, and whether transmission is occurring locally. It may also help link detections in New Zealand with outbreaks in Australia or elsewhere along regional bird-migration routes. The arrival of H5N1 is unlikely to be the end of the story. International experience suggests further incursions may occur as migratory birds continue to move through the region. The challenge therefore shifts from trying to prevent the virus from arriving to detecting new incursions quickly and managing their consequences. The coming weeks will be important in establishing whether this is an isolated detection or the first sign of wider circulation. New Zealand has the benefit of advance warning and extensive international experience. The priority now is to put those lessons into action

analysis.brief_en: New Zealand has confirmed its first case of the highly pathogenic avian influenza virus H5N1, marking a significant but anticipated milestone. The virus has been detected in wildlife, including seabirds and critically endangered species, with current detection rates remaining low. Authorities have been preparing for this event by strengthening surveillance, diagnostic capabilities, and interagency collaboration. Response efforts focus on determining the extent of infection, enhancing surveillance, and implementing biosecurity measures. A vaccine has been approved and is being deployed for endangered wild birds, though its practical application is limited to captive or managed populations. The risk of transmission is highest in densely populated colonies, potentially affecting other species and domestic animals. Genomic sequencing will play a crucial role in tracking the virus's origin and spread. New Zealand's priority is now to quickly detect and manage new incursions, leveraging international experience to minimize impacts on wildlife and agriculture.

news.source_body_en: New Zealand has confirmed its first case of the highly pathogenic avian influenza virus H5N1, marking a significant but anticipated milestone. The virus has been detected in wildlife, including seabirds and critically endangered species, with current detection rates remaining low. Authorities have been preparing for this event by strengthening surveillance, diagnostic capabilities, and interagency collaboration. Response efforts focus on determining the extent of infection, enhancing surveillance, and implementing biosecurity measures. A vaccine has been approved and is being deployed for endangered wild birds, though its practical application is limited to captive or managed populations. The risk of transmission is highest in densely populated colonies, potentially affecting other species and domestic animals. Genomic sequencing will play a crucial role in tracking the virus's origin and spread. New Zealand's priority is now to quickly detect and manage new incursions, leveraging international experience to minimize impacts on wildlife and agriculture.

news.content_title: Local transmission of H5N1 declared as alarm sounds for local birds, sea lions
news.content: Add us as a preferred source on Google Dreaded local transmission of the deadly H5N1 bird flu has been declared in South Australia, sounding the alarm for avian species around the country and sparking fears for a colony of endangered sea lions, which are also susceptible to the virus. The South Australian government said on Wednesday that 11 new cases of the virus had been detected among greater crested terns, a local species that does not leave the country. CSIRO national laboratory testing underway is expected to confirm the SA results. It is likely that migratory seabirds from the Antarctic brought the virus to Australia and it then spread among terns. Seven detections were made on South Australia’s south-east coast, and four on Kangaroo Island. SA Primary Industries Minister Clare Scriven said results showed it was “very, very likely” the birds were infected with H5N1 virus. Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the virus was believed to be spreading in terns and that with the onset of local transmission, it would spread in local populations. “We do expect with this local transmission there will be further transmission in Australian wildlife,” Collins said. Australia’s chief veterinary officer, Dr Beth Cookson, said little could be done to stem the virus moving around the country. “In the natural environment there are limited feasible actions to contain the spread,” Cookson said. Bird flu viruses have circulated around the globe for decades. H5N1 is a particularly deadly variant and has killed hundreds of millions of birds around the world. It is believed that an outbreak in Australia could spark an environmental disaster, risking extinction of dozens of species including marine mammals such as otters, dolphins and seals that also suffer from infection. Scriven said popular beach tours to the colony of about 1000 sea lions at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island had been halted. The virus has not been detected among the marine mammals, but tours were halted to stop any potential disturbances that could harm the colony. There are also about 100,000 long-nosed fur seals on or around Kangaroo Island. These animals can also contract the virus. “Everyone knows how susceptible the [sea lion] population is, and they are an endangered species,” Scriven said. H5N1 arrived in South America in 2022 and killed more than 30,000 South American sea lions, 17,000 southern elephant seal pups and unknown numbers of porpoises, dolphins and otters, as well as at least 650,000 native birds. More than 13,000 seal pups were killed by the virus on Australia’s sub-Antarctic Heard Island territory, which was more than three-quarters of new births on the island. Conservation groups are calling for the immediate deployment of a $200 million fund to boost wildlife resilience. They argue that while the virus cannot be stopped from spreading among wildlife, investment in habitat restoration and programs to cull feral predators can help native animals survive the outbreak. “With only 12,000 individuals left, the Australian sea lion simply cannot absorb the kind of losses we have seen bird flu inflict on marine mammals overseas,” said Australian Marine Conservation Society campaign director Alexia Wellbelove. “Every colony, every pup, every individual matters when a population is this small. We cannot afford to wait.” Invasive Species Council senior advocate James Johnston said emergency wildlife funds were critical. “We can’t stop bird flu reaching every corner of Australia, but we can give our wildlife a much better chance of surviving it,” he said. The Albanese government committed $113 million to preparations to deal with an H5N1 incursion, with an emphasis on planning to identify an outbreak swiftly and a response to limit its spread. This includes funding to prepare biosecurity officers to respond to an outbreak in farmed poultry, which may involve quarantining farms or districts and restricting transport between locations. Tens of millions of dollars have also been committed to environmental measures such as building pup shelters on Kangaroo Island to help reduce infant mortality in sea lions, removing weeds from islands to improve habitat for seabirds, and funding pre-existing captive breeding programs for endangered species such as the Tasmanian devil, orange-bellied parrot and regent honeyeater. The funds would also pay for teams to remove carcasses of infected animals swiftly to prevent further spread and limit contact between wild and farmed birds. Australia’s unique wildlife, which has evolved in isolation for millions of years, could be particularly vulnerable to H5N1. But little is known about native species’ vulnerability. There have been no detections of the virus in farmed poultry. An outbreak would cause a significant impact on chicken meat and egg production. H5N1 in the United States has caused more than 170 million birds to be culled since 2022, while egg prices had tripled by 2025. H5N1 is not considered a significant risk to human health. However, pet birds and cats usually become extremely ill and die when infected. Dogs are more resistant to the virus and rarely die or become severely ill. The same is believed to be true for rabbits and guinea pigs as well as cows, sheep, pigs and horses. People are encouraged to look out for possible infections in birds and marine mammals. Signs include sudden death or difficulty breathing, standing, walking or flying. Sick animals should not be touched, but their location should be noted, with photos and videos, before calling the bird flu hotline on 1800 675 888. analysis.event: Confirmed local transmission of H5N1 bird flu among greater crested terns, with suspected spread to endangered sea lions; reported by South Australian government and federal officials.

analysis.brief_en: Australia has declared local transmission of the deadly H5N1 bird flu in South Australia, with 11 cases detected among greater crested terns. The virus, likely brought by migratory seabirds, poses a significant threat to wildlife, including endangered sea lions on Kangaroo Island. Federal and state officials acknowledge the virus will spread in local populations, with little that can be done to contain it in the wild. Conservation groups are urging immediate deployment of a $200 million fund to boost wildlife resilience, while the government has committed $113 million for response planning and environmental measures. The outbreak raises concerns about potential extinction risks for vulnerable species, though no cases have been detected in farmed poultry.

news.content: Skip to main content Skip to acknowledgement of country Skip to footer Australian Museum Australian Museum website What's On AM Shop Join & Give Search Menu Home AAP News It's now official: bird flu cases in four states It's now official: bird flu cases in four states Australian General News (Photo: Darren England/AAP PHOTOS) Published 25 July 2026 Author Robyn Wuth and John Kidman Located Brisbane Source Australian Associated Press A petrel found washed up on a coastal island by wildlife rangers has been confirmed positive for the deadly H5 bird flu strain. It's discovery, 75 minutes north by ferry from Brisbane on Moreton Island, is a Queensland first. The highly pathogenic avian influenza has now been detected in four states after being found in Western Australia, South Australia and NSW. The most recent detection involved a petrel washing up on a beach on Queensland's Moreton Island. (Tracey Ferrier/AAP PHOTOS) In all there have been 17 confirmed detections since the disease was first reported in WA on June 20. The latest discovery prompted warnings in Queensland on Friday that the virus could have catastrophic consequences for native wildlife and push vulnerable species closer to extinction. Poultry farmers are also battening down the hatches as the virus spreads. However Department of Primary Industry officials said on Saturday there remained no detections in poultry and nor was there evidence of large-scale deaths in any animals in the state. The risk to human health remains low. Poultry farmers are preparing for the worst as the virus spreads. (Jono Searle/AAP PHOTOS) Queensland Chief Veterinary Officer Dr Allison Crook said the confirmed case had been expected. "We have known that a H5 bird flu detection in Queensland was a matter of when, not if," she said. "We have further escalated our surveillance program ... and are delivering heightened H5 bird flu awareness and engagement activities." Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said on Friday the Commonwealth was chiming in with the poultry industry in a bid to keep the "very virulent" and "highly contagious" strain at bay. Julie Collins says the federal government is doing what it can to keep the virus at bay. (Lukas Coch/AAP PHOTOS) "We've had two outbreaks of the H7 bird flu virus in Australia in the last five years or so, and we've been able to successfully eradicate those by working with industry and governments, state and federal," she noted. That aside, Invasive Species Council policy director Dr Carol Booth told AAP bird flu spread should alarm anyone who cared about native animals. Australia's wildlife was already under intense pressure and H5 bird flu could "tip quite a lot of them much closer to extinction", she said. © 2026 AAP View AAP content Terms & Conditions. analysis.brief_en: Australia has confirmed its first case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5 bird flu) in Queensland, with the virus now detected in four states since its initial appearance in Western Australia on June 20. The latest case involved a petrel found on Moreton Island, marking the 17th confirmed detection nationwide. While the risk to human health remains low, authorities warn of potential catastrophic consequences for native wildlife, with vulnerable species potentially pushed closer to extinction. Poultry farmers are preparing for the worst, though no detections in poultry or large-scale animal deaths have been reported. Federal and state governments are escalating surveillance and working with the industry to contain the virus, drawing on past success in eradicating H7 outbreaks.

analysis.time: Published on 2026-07-26, event reported on 2026-07-27.
analysis.location_and_population: Queensland, Australia.
analysis.event: Australia confirms fourth case of H5N1 in Queensland, with no poultry infections confirmed to date.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Total detections rise to 18, but no poultry cases found; risk level not explicitly stated.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Ongoing surveillance and monitoring; no poultry infections confirmed; source limitation: full original report body reviewed.

analysis.brief_en: Australia has confirmed its fourth case of H5N1 avian influenza in Queensland, bringing the total detections to 18, though no poultry infections have been confirmed. The case was reported on July 27, 2026, with authorities maintaining surveillance and monitoring efforts. The situation remains under investigation, with no immediate impact on poultry production reported. This development highlights the continued spread of H5N1 in native bird populations while the poultry industry remains unaffected so far.

AustraliaACTTasmaniaNorthern TerritoryH5N1 bird flu detected in Victoria near Portland as deadly virus spreads across Australia’s coastlineThe deadly H5N1 bird flu strain has spread again, with authorities confirming another positive detection as the virus continues to move across Australia.Madeline CoveThe Nightly1 Min Read20 hours agoUpdated19 hours ago2CommentsCross IconSaveAnother case of the deadly H5N1 bird flu has been confirmed. Credit: AAPThe deadly H5N1 bird flu strain has now been detected in Victoria, marking another step in the virus’s spread across Australia’s southern coastline.Agriculture Victoria confirmed a greater crested tern found near Portland, in the state’s south-west, tested positive for the highly pathogenic avian influenza strain.The discovery comes just days after authorities confirmed local transmission of H5N1 for the first time in Australia among greater crested terns in South Australia.Sign up to The Nightly's newsletters.Get the first look at the digital newspaper, curated daily stories and breaking headlines delivered to your inbox.Your email address:Email UsGet the NewsletterBy continuing you agree to our Terms and Privacy Policy.The virus first arrived in Australia in June when it was detected in a brown skua at Cape Le Grand National Park near Esperance in Western Australia.Since then, it has spread through migratory seabirds, with further detections including a giant petrel in Western Australia and infected birds at Knights Beach in South Australia, close to the Victorian border.Authorities have since confirmed additional H5N1 cases in Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales and Queensland, as biosecurity agencies continue monitoring the virus’s spread.While the current detections have been confined to wild birds, officials remain on high alert amid concerns the highly contagious strain could threaten Australia’s native wildlife and poultry industry.More to come...Tags: Australia. news.content: Asia - Pacific South Australia says H5 bird flu strain likely spreading locally after 11 new suspected cases identified No H5 bird flu has been detected in commercial poultry in the state or elsewhere in the country Amir Latif Arain 29 July 2026 • Update : 29 July 2026 KARAÇI Authorities in South Australia said Wednesday that it is "very, very likely" that the H5 strain of bird flu is spreading locally after the state identified 11 more suspected cases, local media reported. Of the cases, seven were found in the state's South East and four on Kangaroo Island, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported. While officials are still waiting for final testing results, South Australia's Primary Industries Minister Clare Scriven said it was "extremely likely" to represent "localized distribution" of the virus. The state government expects results from a Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization (CSIRO) testing lab Wednesday or Thursday to verify whether the disease is spreading locally between wild birds. "What we've seen around the world is we can't stop H5 bird flu, and there has of course in every other continent around the world been local transmission," Scriven said. Authorities have temporarily closed Seal Bay to the public to help protect the local sea lion population. Scriven said there has been no detections of H5 bird flu in commercial poultry across the state or the rest of the country. South Australia's first confirmed case of H5 bird flu was in a giant petrel found on June 14. news.content_title: Bird flu: What New Zealand can learn from a US poultry farmer hit with H5N1
news.content: She had noticed water and feed levels were a little off in one of her four chicken houses, each housing 37,000 birds. “My mortality started to pick up, but it wasn’t tremendous,” she said. “It wasn’t anything that would have been earth-shattering, but I really started feeling uneasy on a Friday evening.” By 2 o’clock on Saturday afternoon, HPAI was confirmed. “I think it’s, it’s a little bit of disbelief. I think it’s a little bit of, ‘you know, I’ve done everything I can. I’ve done everything I know to do’,” she said. “It’s an overwhelming feeling because it’s a sense of failure.” All farms within a three kilometre radius were quarantined. “You’re thinking, ‘What did I do wrong? This is impacting me, but it’s now impacting my neighbour as well’. “It’s a pretty traumatic experience to go through, and so it’s changed me as a human being.” The houses were then “depopulated” – the chickens euthanised in situ via “ventilation shutdown plus heat” overseen by state agricultural authorities and a vet. “They actually didn’t expect me to be present during the process itself, and that’s good because you’ve invested yourself into a flock of chickens and it’s hard, regardless.” The hardest time for Cartanza was going in the next day to deal with the remaining feed, surrounded by dead chickens. “It’s a really bad feeling to have to do that,” she said. “I wouldn’t wish it on anybody for certain.” Then came the composting process – the bedding, chickens and other material decomposing within the chicken houses for 14 days to contain the virus, subjected to heat with the temperature monitored, deemed virus-free after 28 days. “Then the cleaning process starts – to get the house cleaned up and disinfected.” How bird flu changed the way she farms After the initial shock, Cartanza wanted to figure out where the virus had come in. “So I kind of put my extension hat on and really started trying to think about that, as far as what could I do to help somebody else.” Still poultry farming, she said she has changed a number of things, aside from maintaining a line of separation between clean and dirty. “Anything outside of where the chickens are is considered dirty. And then once you come into the area where you cross that threshold where the chickens are present, that’s now your clean area.” Aside from footbaths, dedicated footwear, hand sanitiser and signs, each chicken house now has its own toolbox and other equipment. “There’s no reason you’re going to bring something from the outside into this house,” she said. “It’s all about touch points and opportunities where, whether it’s your feet, your hands, or an inanimate object, that virus could be carried into your house.” Cartanza grows organic broilers and said certifiers had allowed them to keep them indoors when they deem the risk is greatest – during peak wild bird migration times. “What tends to happen is people almost get burned out, and they’re like, ‘well, nothing’s happened, you know, it’s no big deal’, and they let their guard down.” It was an “odds game,” she said, and a clearly defined high-level biosecurity plan implemented consistently was key to lowering the odds of getting the virus, noting New Zealand’s “phenomenal biosecurity system”. “I’ve been to New Zealand, I went through the airport, I saw what they did to my shoes, but the [wild migratory] birds, they’re not going through that. “So we have to do whatever we can to prevent that from getting into our poultry houses.”

analysis.brief_en: Australia has confirmed local transmission of the H5N1 bird flu virus among native birds, first detected in June and now observed in greater crested terns in South Australia. Minister Julie Collins announced the findings at a news conference, noting that while no mass mortalities have occurred yet, more wildlife detections are anticipated. The poultry industry remains unaffected, with cases reported in four states. This development raises concerns about potential wider spread, reflecting a global pattern since 2021 where H5N1 has affected wild birds, mammals, poultry, and occasionally humans. Authorities are monitoring the situation closely.

analysis.brief_en: Australian health authorities have confirmed the first case of H5 bird flu on Kangaroo Island in South Australia. The virus has been detected in the local seal population, prompting marine experts to evaluate potential intervention strategies. While the exact number of cases and the full extent of the outbreak remain unspecified, authorities are assessing the situation to determine appropriate measures. The confirmation marks a concerning development for the island's wildlife, with experts carefully balancing the need for intervention against potential ecological impacts. Further details on the scale of the outbreak and any human health risks are still under investigation.

news.content: 顶部 首页 首页 多云 / 29° 隐私 澳大陆各州均检出H5N1型高致病性禽流感病毒 齐鲁晚报·齐鲁壹点 澳大利亚珀斯(资料图) 澳大利亚东南部维多利亚州7月30日报告该州首例野生鸟类感染H5N1型高致病性禽流感病毒,这意味着澳大利亚大陆五个州均已发现该病毒。 维多利亚州农业部门说,在该州沿海城市波特兰附近发现的一只大凤头燕鸥体内检测出H5N1病毒,该市位于州首府墨尔本以西约300公里处。澳大利亚疾病防控中心正在进行进一步的基因检测,以确认检测结果。 维多利亚州首席兽医官格雷姆·库克当天表示,该州已启动紧急动物疫病应对计划,尽可能减少这一高致病性禽流感病毒的影响,尤其是保护受威胁程度高的物种,同时降低家禽养殖的风险。 澳大利亚农业、渔业和林业部长朱莉·柯林斯29日表示,南澳州的大凤头燕鸥之间已发生H5型禽流感病毒的本土传播,但该国禽类养殖业目前尚未受到影响。 今年6月,澳大利亚大陆首次发现H5N1型高致病性禽流感病毒。澳大利亚农业、渔业和林业部官网30日发布数据显示,澳大利亚已在野生海鸟中发现28例确诊的H5型禽流感病毒感染病例,其中西澳大利亚州10例、南澳大利亚州15例、新南威尔士州2例、昆士兰州1例。 (央视新闻) 评论 全部 还没有人评论过,快来抢首评 抢首评 推荐阅读 穷姑娘面试模特,一进房间傻眼,考核方式不堪入目! 挑吃兔 2026.7.07 1505.4万+ 7.10日:德不配位必有灾殃!央视表态仅6天,韩红再迎噩耗,孙浩曝内幕 旅卉聊历史 2026.7.09 322.7万+ 全球1.4亿禽鸟死亡:澳洲开始扑杀,防治无力的致命困局 云景史记 16小时前 133 Neurologists Beg Seniors With Neuropathy: Stop Eating These 3 Foods.Vital Life | SponsoredSponsoredLearn MoreUndo个妓女从业10年后的职场领悟:见过太多的男人,比心理专家还懂得人性 孟德何在 2026.7.13 69.4万+ 投票!Pick你心目中的院短视频创作比武十佳短视频(二) 江南水乡生... 2026.7.13 42.6万+ “滚回你的国家!”新西兰外长“怒喷”华人议员!“英语都说不好!”NZ总理公开谴责!中国驻新西兰大使回应! 小公举爱旅... 16小时前 5.4万 小孩哥徒手攀爬防护网形似“蜘蛛侠”,家长安排写保证书反省,网友:飞檐走壁具象化 三湘都市报 7小时前 7198 43岁演员王凯离世,前一天还在拍戏,今天就离世,死因曝光让人泪目 未央史默 4天前 143.9万+ 20名美国探员出动!格雷厄姆死后被查房,特朗普:净浪费时间 狂人鉴史 2026.7.16 33.4万+ 澳大利亚一书逾期150年后归还:翻修房屋时被发现 图书馆免除罚金 海外网 8小时前 67 7.31日:炮声一响,油价飙涨!澳洲猛地回过神,全国炼油厂就剩俩了 飞龙聊体育 4小时前 86 “开除党籍我也不回,除非抬我尸体!”23岁女护士誓言背后的故事 笔尖视界 3天前 99.5万+ LV诉讼风波持续发酵!央媒发声点破真相,日韩网友态度出奇一致 与君説 2026.7.11 25.6万+ 鸡蛋价格暴涨?南极候鸟带来致命病毒,澳大利亚家禽怎么办 罗刹征伐事... 昨天07:53 154 69岁赵本山现状:三亚养老、每天2包烟、8两酒,与杨少华如出一辙 执笔刻文 前天07:48 70.4万+ “反华妖女”许可馨!回国后叫嚣无人敢动她!下场简直大快人心! 龙哥军事 4天前 331.1万+ 别再一直开制冷!空调这个模式解暑效果更佳 草原古都生... 2026.7.13 43.4万+ 7.30日:菲律宾变天?杜特尔特接班人出现,对华态度曝光,马科斯这下坐不住了 恭山动漫说 7小时前 7407 梅根因“回避”简单问题遭猛烈抨击,粉丝口径惊人一致 马马虎虎 7小时前 637 中国祖辈用“粪水浇菜”几千年了,欧洲科学家却才发现,为什么? analysis.time: Published on 2026-07-30. Event dates: First detection in June 2026; Victoria case reported on July 30, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Australia: Victoria (Portland, near Melbourne), South Australia, Western Australia, New South Wales, and Queensland. Affected population: Wild seabirds, particularly crested terns. No impact on poultry industry reported.
analysis.event: Confirmed detection of H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza virus in wild birds across all five Australian mainland states. Victoria reported its first case on July 30, 2026. South Australia confirmed local transmission among crested terns. Reported by Victoria's Chief Veterinary Officer and Australia's Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 28 confirmed H5 avian influenza cases in wild seabirds: Western Australia (10), South Australia (15), New South Wales (2), Queensland (1). No human infections or impact on poultry industry reported. Risk to threatened bird species noted.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Victoria activated emergency animal disease response plan. Further genetic testing underway. Australia's Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry monitoring situation. No human cases reported. Source limitation: Full original article body was reviewed.

analysis.brief_en: Australia has confirmed H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza in wild birds across all five mainland states, with Victoria reporting its first case on July 30, 2026. The virus was detected in a crested tern near Portland, bringing the total to 28 confirmed cases in wild seabirds across the country. South Australia has confirmed local transmission among crested terns, though the poultry industry remains unaffected. Victoria has activated an emergency animal disease response plan, and further genetic testing is underway. Authorities are focusing on protecting threatened species and minimizing risks to poultry farming. No human infections have been reported.

Authorities are focusing on protecting threatened species and minimizing risks to poultry farming. No human infections have been reported.

elements_zh.time: 发布于 2026-07-30。事件日期:2026 年 6 月首次检测;维多利亚案件于 2026 年 7 月 30 日报道。
elements_zh.location_and_population: 澳大利亚:维多利亚(波特兰,墨尔本附近)、南澳大利亚、西澳大利亚、新南威尔士和昆士兰。受影响的种群:野生海鸟,特别是凤头燕鸥。没有对家禽业造成影响的报告。
elements_zh.event: 已确认在澳大利亚大陆所有五个州的 野生鸟类 中检测到 H5N1 高致病性禽流感 病毒。维多利亚州于 2026 年 7 月 30 日报告了第一例病例。南澳大利亚州确认了当地凤头燕鸥中的 传播。由维多利亚州首席兽医官和澳大利亚农业、渔业和林业部长报告。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 野生海鸟中有 28 例确诊 H5 禽流感 病例:西澳大利亚州(10 例)、南澳大利亚州(15 例)、新南威尔士州(2 例)、昆士兰州(1 例)。没有人类感染或对家禽业影响的报道。注意到受威胁鸟类面临的风险。

news.title_zh: 澳大陆各州均检出H5N1型高致病性禽流感病毒 - SOHU
news.source_body_en: Australia has confirmed H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza in wild birds across all five mainland states, with Victoria reporting its first case on July 30, 2026. The virus was detected in a crested tern near Portland, bringing the total to 28 confirmed cases in wild seabirds across the country. South Australia has confirmed local transmission among crested terns, though the poultry industry remains unaffected. Victoria has activated an emergency animal disease response plan, and further genetic testing is underway. Authorities are focusing on protecting threatened species and minimizing risks to poultry farming. No human infections have been reported.
news.content_zh: 澳大利亚已在大陆所有五个州的 野生鸟类 中确认了 H5N1 高致病性禽流感,维多利亚州于 2026 年 7 月 30 日报告了第一例病例。该病毒是在波特兰附近的一只凤头燕鸥中检测到的,使全国野生海鸟确诊病例总数达到 28 例。南澳大利亚州已确认凤头燕鸥中存在本地 传播,但家禽业并未受到影响。维多利亚州已启动紧急动物疾病应对计划,进一步的基因检测正在进行中。当局正致力于保护受威胁物种并最大限度地降低家禽养殖的风险。尚未有人类感染的报道。

news.content: English | 中文 天维网 导购 生活 天维投资 微财经 走进新西兰 HOT 即时新闻 AI全面渗入新西兰校园,教师担忧损害学生独立思考能力 新西兰警方查获特大跨城“大麻工厂” 逮捕16名外籍涉案人员 奥克兰北岸夫妻家中被害案:嫌凶被控两项谋杀罪和一项谋杀未遂 冷酷命案!奥克兰商人遭网约设局抢劫,被刀刺和车辆碾压后惨死街头 ▲ ▼ ×搜索 天维网 | 惠灵顿▼ 奥克兰(Auckland) 哈密尔顿(Hamilton) 惠灵顿(Wellington) 基督城(Christchurch) 皇后镇(Queenstown) 达尼丁(Dunedin) English | 繁體中文 新闻 论坛 生活 投资 移民 视频 商城 橙页 伙伴 2026年7月30日 星期四 农历:二〇二六丙午年六月一七 13° /9°Auckland ▼ 奥克兰(Auckland)哈密尔顿(Hamilton)惠灵顿(Wellington)基督城(Christchurch)皇后镇(Queenstown)达尼丁(Dunedin) 首页 > 新闻中心 > 纽澳新闻 鸡肉能否安全吃?会传染人类吗?MPI华人前检查官详解H5N1禽流感 作者: Jackie Shan 日期:2026-07-26 12:33 阅读:2880 来源:天维网报道 分享到: 邮箱:news@skykiwi.com 复制 【天维网报道 记者Jackie Shan】今年7月中下旬,惠灵顿地区发现两起野生鸟类由于H5型禽流感死亡案例。这是这种传染性极高的病毒首次在新西兰出现。目前,初级产业部门和保育部迅速采取措施,包括将数十万只走地鸡进行保护性“封控”隔离、给珍稀野生禽类注射疫苗等。 这次疫情是否会对新西兰的禽类养殖构成严重影响?居民消费禽类制品以及蛋制品是否安全?应该如何防范家里的宠物被感染?天维网周日(7月26日)连线新西兰华人、初级产业部前高级检查官Steven Yu先生,对热点问题进行详解。 资料图片,来源:RNZ 问题1:禽流感病毒分为哪几种? Steven Yu:禽流感是一种高度传染性的病毒性疾病,主要感染鸟类。不过,它也可能传播给哺乳动物,包括人类。禽流感主要分为两种类型,高致病性禽流感(HPAI),可导致鸟类出现严重症状,并造成较高的死亡率。包括多种病毒株,例如H5、H7。低致病性禽流感(LPAI)通常不会引起鸟类明显症状,或仅引起轻微症状。但有可能发生变异,演变为高致病性禽流感。 问题2:新西兰这次检出与以往有什么不同? Steven Yu:新西兰检疫部门7月17日证实,在北岛东南部的Wairarapa地区发现的一只本土沼泽鹞鹰被确诊感染H5型高致病性禽流感。这是新西兰境内发现的第二例H5型禽流感病例,促使政府紧急升级地面防疫响应。此前2天,新西兰生物安全局通报在惠灵顿海滩的一只褐贼鸥体内检出了同样的禽流感病毒,是新西兰首次发现H5N1高致病性禽流感疫情。 实际上,低致病性禽流感(LPAI)存在于新西兰的野生鸟类中。新西兰设有持续监测计划,每年检测约2,000份野生鸟类样本。这种禽流感病毒通常不会导致野生鸟类出现明显疾病症状。然而,当低致病性禽流感病毒传入鸡群时,它有可能发生变异,演变为高致病性病毒株。 高致病性禽流感(HPAI)病毒株已在全球传播多年。许多国家每年都会在家禽中发生季节性疫情。 过去20年来,新西兰一直密切监测全球HPAI的传播情况。新西兰生物安全局(及其合作伙伴已建立监测体系,以便及时发现 HPAI 及其他外来动物疫病的传入。 新西兰初级产业部(MPI)前高级检查官Steven Yu。供图 问题3:禽流感病毒通过什么途径传入新西兰? Steven Yu:新西兰对动物产品进有非常严格的检疫。所以不大可能通过进口的途径传入。更可能是野生鸟类自然传播。 初级产业部已经提醒广大市民,如果目击到3只或3只以上生病或死亡的鸟类聚集,请立即拨打外来病虫害及疾病报告热线0800 80 99 66。在上报时,如能提供以下详细信息,将极大有助于专家展开调查:生病或死亡鸟类的常见俗名或具体物种;生病或刚死亡的鸟类数量,以及现场鸟类的总数;GPS定位坐标或其他精确的位置描述;现场生病或死亡鸟类的照片或视频资料。 问题4:新西兰的禽蛋食品是否能安全食用? Steven Yu:消费者应该了解正确烹饪鸡肉和鸡蛋的必要性,确保烹制成熟,鸡肉和鸡蛋就是安全的。禽流感病毒可以通过烹饪杀死,所以食用彻底煮熟的鸡蛋和家禽产品仍然是安全的。生食鸡蛋被认为存在风险,我们建议不要食用生鸡蛋,尤其是对免疫系统脆弱的人群,因为鸡蛋可能含有有害病原体,尤其是沙门氏菌。 褐贼鸥。图片来源:NZ Birds Online深入探索健康问题感冒和流感家禽 问题5:这次禽流感疫情对人类健康是否构成危险? Steven Yu:截至目前,新西兰没有出现人类患病的报告,鸡蛋和鸡肉正常供应,目前食品安全风险极低。虽然H5型禽流感在世界多地引发疫情,但此前从未在新西兰发现。20多年来,新西兰初级产业部(MPI)一直对来自北半球的鸟类进行监测。随着病毒感染了野生鸟类,对种群进行保护至关重要。 比如,为了保护新西兰最濒危的鸟类,新西兰保育部(DOC)正在全力推进禽流感疫苗接种计划,初期覆盖5个最濒危物种中的300只核心繁殖鸟,其中包括极度濒危的鸮鹦鹉和南秧鸡。新西兰最大鸡蛋供应商Mainland Poultry已采取紧急防御措施,将其旗下的数十万只走地鸡进行保护性“封控”隔离。热爱户外生活和新西兰自然风光的朋友也可以不用太担心,政府已经开始对新西兰最受保护的五种鸟类进行疫苗接种。 问题6:禽流感是否会感染人类和其它动物? Steven Yu:人类感染H5型禽流感目前仍然十分罕见。这种疾病通常只发生在与受感染鸟类或其他受感染动物有大量密切接触的人身上。如喜欢到野外和鸟类有亲密或近距离接触的朋友,包括在奥克兰海边喂海鸥、鸭子湖公园喂天鹅。家附近公园喂鸽子的朋友都应该注意一下。 H5型禽流感极不可能在人与人之间传播。然而,病毒会随着时间发生变化,因此保持警惕非常重要。换句话说就是目前没有发现人转人的现象。 在海外,一些哺乳动物,包括美国的奶牛,在接触受感染鸟类后也曾感染禽流感。通过支持性治疗,受感染的牛通常会在2至3周内康复。 在新西兰,鸟类将病毒传播给牛或其他家畜的风险很低。其中一个原因是,新西兰的畜牧业养殖方式与美国有很大不同。 问题7:家养的宠物是否会感染禽流感? Steven Yu:我们华人更关心的应该是我们的宠物会不会被传染。答案是肯定的。猫和狗如果食用或接触受感染的动物,也可能生病。猫的症状会重,可能会导致死亡。狗的反应会轻一点。如果哪位朋友家里有养鸡或养鸟就更要注意。为了保护您的宠物免受禽流感感染,请: ——防止野生鸟类接触宠物的食物和饮水。 ——不要让宠物食用或接触患病或死亡的动物。 ——遛狗时请拴好牵引绳,尤其是在野生鸟类附近。 ——尽量让猫待在室内。 ——如果您的宠物在接触野生鸟类后生病,请将其与儿童及其他动物隔离,并尽快联系兽医。 发生禽流感疫情最明显的症状是短时间内多只鸟突然死亡。其他症状包括:虚弱、发抖;瘫痪;呼吸困难;协调能力下降;失明;腹泻。家禽(如鸡、火鸡)通常比野生鸟类表现出更严重的症状,包括:精神萎靡;食欲下降;头部下垂;呼吸困难;动作不协调。如果看到天鹅等原地不停地转圈圈要立即向初级产业部报告,拨打报告热线0800 80 99 66。 版权声明1. 未经《新西兰天维网》书面许可,对于《新西兰天维网》拥有版权、编译和/或其他知识产权的任何内容,任何人不得复制、转载、摘编或在非《新西兰天维网》所属的服务器上做镜像或以其他任何方式进行使用,否则将追究法律责任。2. 在《新西兰天维网》上转载的新闻,版权归新闻原信源所有,新闻内容并不代表本网立场。 版权声明1. 未经《新西兰天维网》书面许可,对于《新西兰天维网》拥有版权、编译和/或其他知识产权的任何内容,任何人不得复制、转载、摘编或在非《新西兰天维网》所属的服务器上做镜像或以其他任何方式进行使用,否则将追究法律责任。 2. 在《新西兰天维网》上转载的新闻,版权归新闻原信源所有,新闻内容并不代表本网立场。 相关推荐 注意!南岛先暖后寒,大雪强风周末来袭 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 12:19 AI全面渗入新西兰校园,教师担忧损害学生独立思考能力 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 11:45 新西兰警方查获特大跨城“大麻工厂” 逮捕16名外籍涉案人员 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 11:23 奥克兰北岸夫妻家中被害案:嫌凶被控两项谋杀罪和一项谋杀未遂 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:56 基督城佳丽加冕新西兰环球小姐 11月参加全球总决赛 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:46 注意!澳洲:H5禽流感开始在野生鸟类间本土传播 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:33 “滚回你的国家!”NZ优先党党魁怒呛华人议员,称其“连英语都说不好”!中国驻新西兰大使回应! 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:26 持枪威胁抢走大众车 奥克兰20岁男子落网 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:19 突发!新西兰知名连锁设计师品牌宣布:即将关门停业! 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:04 员工首日即享年假病假!新西兰《雇佣休假立法案》通过三读 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:03 新闻评论须知 · 请您文明上网、理性发言 · 尊重网上道德,承担一切因您的行为而直接或间接引起的法律责任 · 您的留言只代表个人意见,不代表本站立场 · 天维网拥有管理笔名和留言的一切权利 · 您在天维网留言板发表的言论,天维网有权在网站内转载或引用 · 天维网新闻留言板管理人员有权保留或删除其管辖留言中的任意内容 · 参与本留言即表明您已经阅读并接受上述条款 验证码: × 用户名或者登录密码错误 登 录 创建新的通行证账户 忘记密码 查看所有评论 共( 条) closeAdvertisementsskykiwi_skykiwi [Dynamic Article]-20260730-09:08CANCELNEXT VIDEOplay_arrowvolume_mute AD PausePlay% buffered00:0000:0000:00UnmuteMutePlayclose /HOT热搜榜 新西兰道路惊魂50小时:全国连发致命车祸致7人死亡 【科普帖】新西兰冬天那种“刺骨的冰冷”,到底来自哪里? Steven Yu:禽流感是一种高度传染性的病毒性疾病,主要感染鸟类。不过,它也可能传播给哺乳动物,包括人类。禽流感主要分为两种类型,高致病性禽流感(HPAI),可导致鸟类出现严重症状,并造成较高的死亡率。包括多种病毒株,例如H5、H7。低致病性禽流感(LPAI)通常不会引起鸟类明显症状,或仅引起轻微症状。但有可能发生变异,演变为高致病性禽流感。 问题2:新西兰这次检出与以往有什么不同? Steven Yu:新西兰检疫部门7月17日证实,在北岛东南部的Wairarapa地区发现的一只本土沼泽鹞鹰被确诊感染H5型高致病性禽流感。这是新西兰境内发现的第二例H5型禽流感病例,促使政府紧急升级地面防疫响应。此前2天,新西兰生物安全局通报在惠灵顿海滩的一只褐贼鸥体内检出了同样的禽流感病毒,是新西兰首次发现H5N1高致病性禽流感疫情。 实际上,低致病性禽流感(LPAI)存在于新西兰的野生鸟类中。新西兰设有持续监测计划,每年检测约2,000份野生鸟类样本。这种禽流感病毒通常不会导致野生鸟类出现明显疾病症状。然而,当低致病性禽流感病毒传入鸡群时,它有可能发生变异,演变为高致病性病毒株。 高致病性禽流感(HPAI)病毒株已在全球传播多年。许多国家每年都会在家禽中发生季节性疫情。 过去20年来,新西兰一直密切监测全球HPAI的传播情况。新西兰生物安全局(及其合作伙伴已建立监测体系,以便及时发现 HPAI 及其他外来动物疫病的传入。 新西兰初级产业部(MPI)前高级检查官Steven Yu。供图 问题3:禽流感病毒通过什么途径传入新西兰? Steven Yu:新西兰对动物产品进有非常严格的检疫。所以不大可能通过进口的途径传入。更可能是野生鸟类自然传播。 初级产业部已经提醒广大市民,如果目击到3只或3只以上生病或死亡的鸟类聚集,请立即拨打外来病虫害及疾病报告热线0800 80 99 66。在上报时,如能提供以下详细信息,将极大有助于专家展开调查:生病或死亡鸟类的常见俗名或具体物种;生病或刚死亡的鸟类数量,以及现场鸟类的总数;GPS定位坐标或其他精确的位置描述;现场生病或死亡鸟类的照片或视频资料。 问题4:新西兰的禽蛋食品是否能安全食用? Steven Yu:消费者应该了解正确烹饪鸡肉和鸡蛋的必要性,确保烹制成熟,鸡肉和鸡蛋就是安全的。禽流感病毒可以通过烹饪杀死,所以食用彻底煮熟的鸡蛋和家禽产品仍然是安全的。生食鸡蛋被认为存在风险,我们建议不要食用生鸡蛋,尤其是对免疫系统脆弱的人群,因为鸡蛋可能含有有害病原体,尤其是沙门氏菌。 褐贼鸥。图片来源:NZ Birds Online深入探索健康问题感冒和流感家禽 问题5:这次禽流感疫情对人类健康是否构成危险? Steven Yu:截至目前,新西兰没有出现人类患病的报告,鸡蛋和鸡肉正常供应,目前食品安全风险极低。虽然H5型禽流感在世界多地引发疫情,但此前从未在新西兰发现。20多年来,新西兰初级产业部(MPI)一直对来自北半球的鸟类进行监测。随着病毒感染了野生鸟类,对种群进行保护至关重要。 比如,为了保护新西兰最濒危的鸟类,新西兰保育部(DOC)正在全力推进禽流感疫苗接种计划,初期覆盖5个最濒危物种中的300只核心繁殖鸟,其中包括极度濒危的鸮鹦鹉和南秧鸡。新西兰最大鸡蛋供应商Mainland Poultry已采取紧急防御措施,将其旗下的数十万只走地鸡进行保护性“封控”隔离。热爱户外生活和新西兰自然风光的朋友也可以不用太担心,政府已经开始对新西兰最受保护的五种鸟类进行疫苗接种。 问题6:禽流感是否会感染人类和其它动物? Steven Yu:人类感染H5型禽流感目前仍然十分罕见。这种疾病通常只发生在与受感染鸟类或其他受感染动物有大量密切接触的人身上。如喜欢到野外和鸟类有亲密或近距离接触的朋友,包括在奥克兰海边喂海鸥、鸭子湖公园喂天鹅。家附近公园喂鸽子的朋友都应该注意一下。 H5型禽流感极不可能在人与人之间传播。然而,病毒会随着时间发生变化,因此保持警惕非常重要。换句话说就是目前没有发现人转人的现象。 在海外,一些哺乳动物,包括美国的奶牛,在接触受感染鸟类后也曾感染禽流感。通过支持性治疗,受感染的牛通常会在2至3周内康复。 在新西兰,鸟类将病毒传播给牛或其他家畜的风险很低。其中一个原因是,新西兰的畜牧业养殖方式与美国有很大不同。 问题7:家养的宠物是否会感染禽流感? Steven Yu:我们华人更关心的应该是我们的宠物会不会被传染。答案是肯定的。猫和狗如果食用或接触受感染的动物,也可能生病。猫的症状会重,可能会导致死亡。狗的反应会轻一点。如果哪位朋友家里有养鸡或养鸟就更要注意。为了保护您的宠物免受禽流感感染,请: ——防止野生鸟类接触宠物的食物和饮水。 ——不要让宠物食用或接触患病或死亡的动物。 ——遛狗时请拴好牵引绳,尤其是在野生鸟类附近。 ——尽量让猫待在室内。 ——如果您的宠物在接触野生鸟类后生病,请将其与儿童及其他动物隔离,并尽快联系兽医。 发生禽流感疫情最明显的症状是短时间内多只鸟突然死亡。其他症状包括:虚弱、发抖;瘫痪;呼吸困难;协调能力下降;失明;腹泻。家禽(如鸡、火鸡)通常比野生鸟类表现出更严重的症状,包括:精神萎靡;食欲下降;头部下垂;呼吸困难;动作不协调。如果看到天鹅等原地不停地转圈圈要立即向初级产业部报告,拨打报告热线0800 80 99 66。 版权声明1. 未经《新西兰天维网》书面许可,对于《新西兰天维网》拥有版权、编译和/或其他知识产权的任何内容,任何人不得复制、转载、摘编或在非《新西兰天维网》所属的服务器上做镜像或以其他任何方式进行使用,否则将追究法律责任。2. 在《新西兰天维网》上转载的新闻,版权归新闻原信源所有,新闻内容并不代表本网立场。 版权声明1. 未经《新西兰天维网》书面许可,对于《新西兰天维网》拥有版权、编译和/或其他知识产权的任何内容,任何人不得复制、转载、摘编或在非《新西兰天维网》所属的服务器上做镜像或以其他任何方式进行使用,否则将追究法律责任。 2. 在《新西兰天维网》上转载的新闻,版权归新闻原信源所有,新闻内容并不代表本网立场。 相关推荐 注意!南岛先暖后寒,大雪强风周末来袭 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 12:19 AI全面渗入新西兰校园,教师担忧损害学生独立思考能力 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 11:45 新西兰警方查获特大跨城“大麻工厂” 逮捕16名外籍涉案人员 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 11:23 奥克兰北岸夫妻家中被害案:嫌凶被控两项谋杀罪和一项谋杀未遂 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:56 基督城佳丽加冕新西兰环球小姐 11月参加全球总决赛 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:46 注意!澳洲:H5禽流感开始在野生鸟类间本土传播 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:33 “滚回你的国家!”NZ优先党党魁怒呛华人议员,称其“连英语都说不好”!中国驻新西兰大使回应! 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:26 持枪威胁抢走大众车 奥克兰20岁男子落网 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:19 突发!新西兰知名连锁设计师品牌宣布:即将关门停业! 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:04 员工首日即享年假病假!新西兰《雇佣休假立法案》通过三读 纽澳新闻 | 综合2026-07-30 10:03 新闻评论须知 · 请您文明上网、理性发言 · 尊重网上道德,承担一切因您的行为而直接或间接引起的法律责任 · 您的留言只代表个人意见,不代表本站立场 · 天维网拥有管理笔名和留言的一切权利 · 您在天维网留言板发表的言论,天维网有权在网站内转载或引用 · 天维网新闻留言板管理人员有权保留或删除其管辖留言中的任意内容 · 参与本留言即表明您已经阅读并接受上述条款 验证码: × 用户名或者登录密码错误 登 录 创建新的通行证账户 忘记密码 查看所有评论 共( 条) closeAdvertisementsskykiwi_skykiwi [Dynamic Article]-20260730-09:08CANCELNEXT VIDEOplay_arrowvolume_mute AD PausePlay% buffered00:0000:0000:00UnmuteMutePlayclose /HOT热搜榜 新西兰道路惊魂50小时:全国连发致命车祸致7人死亡 【科普帖】新西兰冬天那种“刺骨的冰冷”,到底来自哪里? analysis.time: Publication date: 2026-07-26. Event date: Mid-to-late July 2026, with confirmed cases on July 17 and July 15.
analysis.location_and_population: New Zealand, specifically Wellington region (Wairarapa area) and North Island southeast. Affected populations include wild birds (swamp harrier, brown skua), free-range chickens (hundreds of thousands under protective isolation), and endangered bird species (kakapo, weka).
analysis.event: Confirmed outbreak of H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza in New Zealand for the first time. Two wild bird deaths reported (July 15 and 17), prompting government response including isolation of poultry and vaccination of endangered species. No human cases reported.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Cases: At least 2 confirmed wild bird infections (H5N1). No human infections. No deaths reported in humans. Risk assessment: Low risk to human health; no person-to-person transmission detected. High risk to bird populations, prompting protective measures for poultry and endangered species.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Government response includes protective isolation of hundreds of thousands of free-range chickens, vaccination of 300 core breeding birds of 5 endangered species, and public reporting hotline (0800 80 99 66). Uncertainty: No information on long-term spread or mutation potential; ongoing monitoring of wild birds and poultry.

analysis.brief_en: New Zealand has confirmed its first outbreak of H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza, with two wild bird deaths reported in mid-July 2026. The virus was detected in a swamp harrier in Wairarapa and a brown skua in Wellington. Authorities have responded by isolating hundreds of thousands of free-range chickens and vaccinating endangered species like the kakapo. No human cases have been reported, and officials emphasize that properly cooked poultry and eggs remain safe. The risk of human-to-human transmission is considered low, but pet owners are advised to prevent contact between pets and wild birds. The outbreak highlights New Zealand's first detection of this virus in two decades.

今次是6月以来澳洲第四个州确认出现H5N1禽流感。(法新社资料图片) 澳洲昆士兰州确认一宗高致病性H5N1禽流感病毒感染个案,是6月以来澳洲第四个州确认出现H5N1禽流感。 感染病毒的是一只迁徙海鸟,昆士兰州的家禽目前未检测到病毒,亦没有出现动物大规模死亡的情况。 西澳州一只褐贼鸥,上月感染H5N1死亡,是澳洲大陆首次确认发现H5N1禽流感病毒,至今全澳洲确诊18宗个案,分别出现在西澳州、南澳州、新南威尔士州和昆士兰州。当局表示,正加紧调查病毒的传播途径。 编辑:许敬轩 澳洲昆士兰州确认一宗H5N1禽流感病毒感染个案 全部本地大中华国际财经体育 解放军在中国黄岩岛领海领空及周边海空域开展战备警巡 2026-07-31 HKT 04:19 今次是6月以来澳洲第四个州确认出现H5N1禽流感。(法新社资料图片) 澳洲昆士兰州确认一宗高致病性H5N1禽流感病毒感染个案,是6月以来澳洲第四个州确认出现H5N1禽流感。 感染病毒的是一只迁徙海鸟,昆士兰州的家禽目前未检测到病毒,亦没有出现动物大规模死亡的情况。 西澳州一只褐贼鸥,上月感染H5N1死亡,是澳洲大陆首次确认发现H5N1禽流感病毒,至今全澳洲确诊18宗个案,分别出现在西澳州、南澳州、新南威尔士州和昆士兰州。当局表示,正加紧调查病毒的传播途径。 编辑:许敬轩 澳洲昆士兰州确认一宗H5N1禽流感病毒感染个案 全部本地大中华国际财经体育 解放军在中国黄岩岛领海领空及周边海空域开展战备警巡 2026-07-31 HKT 04:19 analysis.time: Publication date: 2026-07-26. Event date: Not specified in the evidence, but the infection was confirmed in June 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Affected population: A migratory seabird. Poultry in Queensland have not tested positive for the virus.
analysis.event: Confirmed case of highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza virus infection in a migratory seabird in Queensland. This is the fourth state in Australia to confirm an H5N1 case since June 2026.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Cases: 18 confirmed cases across Australia (Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales, and Queensland). Deaths: One death reported in Western Australia (a brown skua). No mass mortality in animals reported. Risk: Not explicitly stated in the evidence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Authorities are accelerating investigations into the virus transmission routes. No mass mortality or poultry infection reported in Queensland. The source is a full original report body.

analysis.brief_en: Australia's Queensland state has confirmed a case of highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza in a migratory seabird, marking the fourth state in the country to report an H5N1 infection since June 2026. The infected bird is a migratory species, and no poultry in Queensland have tested positive for the virus. This brings the total number of confirmed H5N1 cases in Australia to 18, with previous cases reported in Western Australia, South Australia, and New South Wales. Authorities are intensifying efforts to investigate the transmission pathways of the virus. No mass animal mortality has been observed in the affected areas.

supplementary_news.content: Avian Flu Diary Covering Pandemic and Seasonal Flu, Emerging Infectious Diseases, public health, community & Individual preparedness. NOTE: All AFD blogs are written by a human - any mistakes are solely mine. Thursday, July 30, 2026 Australia: CSIRO Reports 4 H5 Positive Crested Tern Samples from Kangaroo Island Credit Wikipedia#19,270No sooner has I posted my last blog when the following statement was posted on the Australian government website:30 July 2026Attributable to Australian Chief Veterinary Officer, Dr Beth Cookson:Testing at CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness (ACDP) has returned four positive results in crested terns, from Kangaroo Island, South Australia.There have now been 33 confirmed or presumed positive detections of H5 bird flu in Australia.All of these have been wild seabirds found in coastal locations.There remains no evidence of any mass mortality events and there are no detections in poultry or in our agricultural production system. The risk to human health remains low.While not particularly surprising given its proximity to the other SA confirmed seabirds, this is a concern because Kangaroo Island is home to a number of marine mammals which are known to be susceptible to avian flu, including:Australian sea lion.Australian fur seal.New Zealand fur seal.Bottlenose dolphin and common dolphin. Last October H5N1 was detected on Australia's Heard Island - which we recently revisited in Preprint: Mass mortality of southern elephant seals during multi-species outbreak of HPAI H5N1 on sub-Antarctic Heard Island - which reported:Drone surveys revealed mass mortality in southern elephant seals, with 8,573 pups (62%) recorded dead across Heard Island by the final surveys. Mortality increased at an average rate of 5.6% per day in a subset of harems, and the highest observed mortality in a harem was 97%. Based on the average (76%) mortality in the final surveys, total estimated pup mortality at Heard Island was 13,359 (from a total population of 17,364 pups), though this may be an underestimate as mortality was ongoing at this time. HPAI was detected in six of nine species tested and, we suspect, led to elevated mortality in king and gentoo penguins.While there is currently no evidence of spillover into Kangaroo Island's marine or terrestrial mammalian population, this is another worrisome milestone for HPAI as it spreads across Oceania. Australia: H5N1 Reaches Victoria - SA `Suspect' Count Rises (n=24) #19,269A few hours ago Victoria announced their first H5N1 detection, once again in a greater crested tern, this time found in Portland. We've two announcements, first from Agriculture Victoria, and second by Australian Chief Veterinary Officer, Dr Beth Cookson announcing the confirmation from CSIRO. H5N1 avian influenza strain detected in Victoria30 July 2026The high pathogenicity avian influenza H5N1 strain (H5 bird flu) has been detected in Victoria.Victoria’s Chief Veterinary Officer Dr Graeme Cooke said this detection is a result of Australia’s response to H5 bird flu, with the Victorian Government undertaking surveillance for the disease and working closely with the Commonwealth, interstate jurisdictions and industry partners.‘Preliminary testing has indicated H5 bird flu in a single greater crested tern found in Portland. Further genetic testing is underway at CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness at Geelong to formally confirm this result.’ Dr Cooke said.‘This follows confirmation of the disease in seabirds in Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales and Queensland, and the national decision that H5 bird flu is no longer technically feasible to eradicate in wildlife.’‘Following weeks of enhanced readiness, we have now enacted Victoria’s State Emergency Animal Disease Response Plan. Based on international experience, this H5 variant differs from previous strains and has been known to cause large numbers of deaths in wild birds and some mammals.’‘Our plans aim to limit impacts where possible particularly on our most threatened species, while also supporting our farmers and reducing risk to domestic and commercial poultry.‘We need Victorians to avoid contact with sick or dead wildlife, record what they see and report it. Early reporting gives us the best chance to reduce the impacts of the disease,’ Dr Cooke said. (Continue . . . ) 30 July 2026Attributable to Australian Chief Veterinary Officer, Dr Beth Cookson:Testing at CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness (ACDP) has confirmed H5 bird flu in a greater crested tern, found in Portland in Victoria.This is the first case in the state of Victoria.There have now been 29 confirmed or presumed positive detections of H5 bird flu in Australia.All of these have been wild seabirds found in coastal locations.There remains no evidence of any mass mortality events and there are no detections in poultry or in our agricultural production system.The risk to human health remains lowMeanwhile, South Australia has confirmed a 15th case (a Giant Petrel), and reports an additional 24 suspect cases are pending confirmation by CSIRO.Current situationSouth Australia’s first confirmed detection of H5 bird flu was in a wild migratory bird (southern giant petrel) on Wednesday, 24 June at Knights Beach at Port Elliot on the Fleurieu Peninsula.Further confirmed detections include a giant petrel (8 July at Hardwicke Bay, Yorke Peninsula); a southern giant petrel (10 July at Emu Bay, Kangaroo Island); a northern giant petrel (10 July at Port Vincent, Yorke Peninsula); three greater crested terns (10 July at Robe, Limestone Coast; 26 July at Semaphore, metro Adelaide; and 26 July at Robe, Limestone Coast); seven greater crested terns (28 July at Cape Jaffa, Port MacDonnell and Southend, Lower South East); and a giant petrel (30 July at Port Lincoln, Eyre Peninsula).A further 24 suspected H5 bird flu detections are undergoing further confirmatory testing at the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness in Victoria.The strain of virus is consistent with the strain detected in the Southern Indian Ocean Sub-Antarctic Territories, including Heard Island.This strain has not been detected in poultry and has not become established in any part of Australia.Up-to-date national information is available at birdflu.gov.au.Although the official numbers remain reassuring low (n=29), they undoubtedly represent only a small fraction of actual H5 burden on wildlife in Australia. Two weeks ago, we looked at the growing gap between reported events, prioritized and investigated cases, and lab testing in Western Australia. Graphic generated by GeminiI've not seen an update from WA since July 17th - where total reports then exceeded 1,800 - and sadly, other states have not provided this sort of granular detail. But it is a fairly safe assumption that similar backlogs exist around the nation. Obviously, no surveillance and testing program can hope to capture more than a small fraction of the HPAI activity in birds or animals in the wild. At best, it can give us some idea as to the spread, intensity, and host range of HPAI H5 across the continent. And right now, based on available data, H5N1 appears to be making significant inroads down under. Wednesday, July 29, 2026 EID Journal Dispatch: Seroprevalence of Influenza A(H5N1) Virus in Domestic Cats at Epicenter of Dairy Cattle Outbreaks, California, USA, 2024–2026 Seropositive cats around HPAI Infected Dairy Farm#19,268We've known for more than 2 decades that cats - both large and small - are susceptible to HPAI H5 infection (see 2004 CIDRAP Report) and have seen scattered reports over the years (see 2015's HPAI H5: Catch As Cats Can).Until relatively recently, those reports were fairly rare, and mainly came from zoo animals fed on a diet of raw chicken. But since the emergence of a new, more transmissible clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus in 2021, the number of companion animals (and other mammals) reported to be infected has risen sharply.While undoubtedly underreported, more than 20% of all of the mammalian wildlife detections reported in the United States (180 of 813 USDA reports) over the past 4 years have been among felines. Many have been reported in and around dairy and poultry farms (see EID Journal: HPAI A(H5N1) Clade 2.3.4.4b Virus Infection in Domestic Dairy Cattle and Cats, United States, 2024).While many cats infected with HPAI sicken and die, others - based on seroprevalence studies (see Eurosurveillance: (HPAI) H5 virus Exposure in Domestic & Rural Stray Cats, the Netherlands, October 2020 to June 2023) - are likely only mildly affected and survive.Previously, we've seen evidence of cattle-to-bird-to-cat transmission of avian flu, large outbreaks in animal shelters suggesting cat-to-cat transmission (H7N2), and limited evidence of cat-to-human transmission (see here and here). All of which brings us to a new dispatch, published yesterday in the EID Journal, which reports a 25% seropositivity rate among (n=12) cats sampled within 2 km of infected dairy farms, while no cats were seropositive further away (n=61).While this is just one small, geographically limited, study the authors state: "Proximity to dairy farms in counties experiencing outbreaks may be a risk factor for H5N1 spillover to indoor and outdoor domestic cats."I've only posted the highlights, follow the link to read the report in its entirety.Volume 32, Number 9—September 2026DispatchSeroprevalence of Influenza A(H5N1) Virus in Domestic Cats at Epicenter of Dairy Cattle Outbreaks, California, USA, 2024–2026 Ian G. Bemis, Ismaila Shittu, Jacob F. Gomez, Esther A. Fadaka, Sofia Perez, Gregory C. Gray, and Kristen K. Coleman AbstractWe conducted a serologic study of domestic cats near the epicenter of the dairy cattle outbreaks of influenza A(H5N1) in California, USA. Three of the 12 cats sampled within 2 km of farms had neutralizing antibodies against H5N1 virus.
